extracted.intended_audience: aspiring humor writers, stand-up comedians, speechwriters, and performers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and performing comedic material across formats (one-liners, anecdotes, speeches, columns, stand-up), emphasizing joke structure, audience targeting, editing, and brainstorming/testing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (cardinal rule of comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise is one of the most universally accepted formulas for humor; the need for surprise is the one cardinal rule in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use misdirection: set up an expectation then deliver an unexpected twist. Examples: setup -> punchline; sometimes sacrifice grammar or logic to achieve the unexpected. Scoring notes: degree of surprise correlates with laugh potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority (audience feels superior)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh when we feel superior; comedy often elicits laughter by allowing the audience to feel smarter or above the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose targets and material that permit the audience to feel superior. Ensure the audience 'equally disfavors your target' so the joke is acceptable. Avoid targets that alienate the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup → Punchline structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is a story where a setup prepares a line of thought and the punchline provides the surprise ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three-part structure (setup, anticipation, punchline) is standard. Keep setups realistic; build toward a surprise payoff. Avoid revealing key words in the setup and save the funniest word for the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: THREES formula (six required elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether one-liner or long piece, six elements are required (THREES): Target, Hostility, Realism, Exaggeration, Emotion, and Surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the acronym THREES to evaluate a bit: does it have a clear target, appropriate hostility, a realistic basis, exaggeration that signals joke, emotional buildup, and a surprise ending? The prescribed order can be challenged but all elements are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (directed humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is criticism cloaked as entertainment and directed at a specific target; it often reaffirms audience's hostilities and prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a clear target for the joke and verify the audience will accept ridicule of that target. Practice exercises: list hostile targets and freely associate. Scoring: clarity and appropriateness of target to audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostility (tension/edge in humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostility creates tension and is often the driving emotion behind many jokes, including nihilistic humor that ridicules everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hostility to build anticipation but avoid going beyond what the audience tolerates. Topics: money, anxieties, taboo subjects can be rich sources if audience alignment exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism (truth basis for setup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most good jokes state a bitter truth; realism provides the basis the audience can associate with before exaggeration creates the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the premise is true and relatable for the audience. Realism is typically the setup; exaggeration is the payoff. Avoid setups that are implausible or unfamiliar to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (hyperbole signals joke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is an effective comedic tool; it changes perception of reality and signals that the material is a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperbole, blatant distortion, and overstated figures to make absurdity clear. But 'outrageous doesn't mean creative'—ensure exaggeration serves the surprise and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion (build tension/anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotion—often anger or hostility—is used to create anticipation that the punch will release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include pregnant pauses and asking audience questions. The buildup of emotion increases payoff; measure whether the audience feels the intended tension before the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEE for premises (Truth, Emotion, Explicitness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three criteria determine whether a premise properly sets up the punchline: T = TRUTH, E = EMOTION, E = EXPLICITNESS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A solid premise should be reality-based (truth), carry emotion (usually anger/hostility), and be specific and readily understood by others. Use TEE to vet setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of Three / Triples
rubrics_metrics.description: The magical number is three: establish a pattern with two similar items; the third breaks it for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triples typically follow SAP: Setup, Anticipation (the triple), Punch line. Use truth, emotion, explicitness to tee up the triple; examples and quotations illustrate effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play on Words (POW) and Double Entendre
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordplay techniques like puns and double entendres exploit ambiguous meanings for humorous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include linguistic devices (Teaming, Tom Swiftys, sniglets). Note: many examples are English-centric; ensure wordplay translates to your language/audience. Avoid overreliance on lowest-form puns unless novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Takeoff / Simple Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a standard expression or cliché and draw an outrageous, literal, or unexpected conclusion from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-known phrases as set-ups and then 'take off' into an absurd or revealing interpretation. The takeoff can include double entendres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverses (unexpected switch)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reverse adds a contradictory tag line or switches the audience's point of view to create surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain surprise, drop a misdirecting clue to push the audience in a false direction. Reverses often require a prominent clue that misleads before the switch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of words / Aggressive editing
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed joke uses as few words as possible, preserves the funniest part until the end, and cuts nonessential words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mantra: Make every word work. Apply successive drafts to cut nonessentials; final draft should remove every nonessential word. Humor and Duration Principle: shorter path to the joke is funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reveal key words in setup; save funniest word for the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-constructed jokes do not reveal key words in the setup and place the funniest/ surprise word at the end of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure sentences so the payoff word is final; avoid trailing words after the punchline. Editing should eliminate words that undercut the surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brainstorming methods (association & listing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common brainstorming methods include association and listing to examine a topic from every angle and generate material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use association (teaming dissimilar items), listing (rule of ten in, nine out), mindmapping, and collecting clichés/phrases to find humor possibilities. Keep a personal humor journal and clip material from media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity principle and rewriting (write/test/rewrite)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of ten in, nine out: generate many ideas; professionals write three times what's needed, then rewrite and discard until the best remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test material on small audiences, rewrite heavily, and be prepared to discard most output. Practice/testing is essential—'Test, Test, Test.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Workarounds for writer's block
rubrics_metrics.description: Four tools for busting through humor block: work backwards (write the punchline first), look for opposites, talk instead of writing, and imagine (visualize) instead of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record yourself, create mental movies, or construct the final line first then build the setup. These methods help generate unexpected associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance persona and consistency (MAP / MAPP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the material, audience, performer, and purpose (MAPP) — maintain a consistent performer persona that matches the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only after knowing audience and persona traits should you write material. 'Stand-up is a funny man doing material, not a man doing funny material. The personality—the character—not the joke—is primary.' Evaluate consistency and comfort for performer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience management and testing in live settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Test material with small audiences; in small rooms find one laugher and engage them; use social cues (boss/laugh leader) to license group laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing for small groups, identify a loud laugher and elicit their response (look/wink). Get friendly with senior figures whose laughter gives permission to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech-specific constraints and guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: For humorous speeches: be funny, make it comfortable for the speaker and audience, personalize/localize humor, never apologize or explain jokes; a speech should not exceed twenty minutes (~3,000 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal speaking rate ~2.5 words/sec; best sentence length for a speech ~14 words. Personalize material even if fabricated; avoid explaining jokes or apologizing ('This may not be funny...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-deprecation appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-deprecating humor is often safe and effective; inviting people to laugh at you while you laugh at yourself helps audience rapport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-deprecation to humanize the speaker. It should be genuine and not undermine performer credibility or comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and phonetic choices (word sounds matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain sounds (e.g., k sounds) and word phonetics can be inherently funny and aid a joke's impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words with humor-friendly sounds and vivid imagery; consider tested patterns (examples given: 'cookie' vs 'tomato'). Assess whether chosen words increase comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and vivid imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid general, abstract phrases; use concrete, specific, graphic descriptions that stimulate the senses and aid visualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: rewrite general phrases (grab some food → specify Snickers bar). Specific references increase the joke's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format/market awareness (write for the venue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different markets require different forms: columns, greeting cards, t-shirts, advertising, sitcoms, stand-up, speeches all have format expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor length and style (e.g., print columns 500–700 words weekly). Learn market conventions and adapt jokes to format constraints and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-explaining and apologizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Never apologize or explain a joke (e.g., 'This may not be funny, but...'); explanations lower expectations and undercut laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust edits and testing; if material needs explanation, it likely needs rewriting. Don't coach the audience to expect weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor testing & iteration (practice habits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals continuously test material, maintain a humor diary, practice writing and performing, and iterate extensively until items that work remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habits: watch sitcoms, read humor, keep a humor journal, perform regularly, and treat writing as iterative craft—write many, keep few.
